# Overview

This document summarizes the Time Series Growth Curves (TSGC) package for R. The package implements time series growth curve methods founded on a dynamic Gompertz model and can be estimated using techniques based on state space models and the Kalman filter reported by Harvey and Kattuman (2020, hence forth HK). The model is suitable for predicting future values of any variable which, when accumulated, is subject to some unknown saturation level. I will be using this package to forecast spikes in weather-induced hospital demand in. First, I will give theoretical background on the TSGC univariate model. Then, I will apply the univariate model using the `tsgc` package to forecast A&E attendance in Scotland, using simulated data. Finally, I will provide theoretical background on how the current `tsgc` package will be expanded to handle multivariate models.

# Theory: Time series growth curves

## Cheat Sheet

| **State variable**         | **Sym.**         | **Description**                                                                                                                |
|----------------------------|------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Saturation level           | $\overline{\mu}$ | Final number of cumulative cases, $\overline{\mu} > 0$                                                                         |
| Cumulative cases           | $Y_t$            | Total number of cases up to time $t$                                                                                           |
| New cases                  | $y_t$            | Daily new cases of outcome, ${\  y}_{t} \  = Y_{t} - {\  Y}_{t - 1}$ or ${\Delta Y}_{t}$                                       |
| Growth rate                | $g_t$            | Growth rate of cumulative cases at time $t$,  $g_{t} \  = \  \frac{{\  y}_{t}}{{\  Y}_{t - 1}}$ or $\Delta \ln {\  Y}_{t - 1}$ |
| Time trend parameter       | $\delta_{t}$     | Log of intercept term in Gompertz model                                                                                        |
| Growth rate of growth rate | $\gamma_{t}$     | Change in log growth rate over time,  $\gamma_{t} \  = \delta_{t} - \delta_{t - 1}$ or ${\Delta \delta}_{t}$                   |

## Deterministic Gompertz Model (Univariate)

First, let us describe a deterministic Gompertz model.

All Gompertz models assume that the cumulative number of cases (aka saturation level) follows a Gompertz growth curve, which has a sigmoidal curve pattern. Given this, the cumulative cases at a given time, $\mu_{t}$, can be written as:

$\mu_{t} = \  \overline{\mu} e x p  \{ \gamma_{0} e^{\gamma t} \}$

where $\overline{\mu}$ is the final unknown saturation level, $\gamma$ is the growth rate, $\gamma_{0}$ is the initial condition relating to $\mu_{0}$ and $\gamma < 0$. Generalised logistic growth curve theory suggests models for $l n \  \mu_{t}^{'}$, (new daily cases) and $l n \  g_{t}$ (cumulative growth rate) at time $t$, where $\mu_{t}^{'} = \frac{d \mu_{t}}{d t}$ and $g_{t} = \  \frac{\mu_{t}^{'}}{\mu_{t}}$ . Deterministic Gompertz growth curves can thus be defined by:

(1) $l n \  \mu_{t}^{'} = \ln {\  \mu}_{t - 1} + \ln {\  g}_{t}$ , $t = 1 , \ldots T$

(2) $l n \  g_{t} = \  \delta + \gamma t + \  \varepsilon_{t}$,

where $\delta$ is the log of the Gompertz model intercept term, defined as $\delta = l n \gamma_{0} \gamma$, $\varepsilon_{t}$ is the random disturbance term and $\gamma > 0$. However the deterministic trend implied by equation (2) is too inflexible for practical time-series modelling in real-time.

## Dynamic Gompertz Model (Univariate)

Let’s replace $\mu_{t}$ with $Y_{t}$, to represent the observed cumulative number of cases on day $t$, where $t = 1 , \ldots T$. We will also replace $\mu_{t}^{'}$ with $y_{t}$, to represent the number of daily new cases, such that $y_{t} = Y_{t} - Y_{t - 1}$ or ${\Delta Y}_{t}$. Instead of modelling $Y_{t}$ or $y_{t}$ directly, we will model the log growth rate of the cumulative level, $Y_{t}$, defined as ${l n \  g}_{t} = l n \left( \frac{y_{t}}{Y_{t - 1}} \right)$ or $l n \  g_{t} = \  l n \  y_{t} - l n \  Y_{t - 1}$. A stochastic-trend is then introduced to $l n \  g_{t}$ to allow the model to dynamically adapt to changes over the course of a wave. Therefore, we can replace equations (1) and (2) with the following dynamic Gompertz time trend model:

(3) $l n \  y_{t} = \ln {\  Y}_{t - 1} + \ln {\  g}_{t}$ , $t = 1 , \ldots T$

(4) $\ln {\  g}_{t} = \delta_{t} + \varepsilon_{t}$ , $\varepsilon_{t} \sim \  N I D ( 0 , \sigma_{\epsilon}^{2} )$

$\delta_{t} = \delta_{t - 1} + \  \gamma_{t - 1} + \eta_{t}$ , $\eta_{t} \sim \  N I D ( 0 , \sigma_{\eta}^{2} )$

$\gamma_{t} = \gamma_{t - 1} + \zeta_{t}$ , $\zeta_{t} \sim \  N I D ( 0 , \sigma_{\zeta}^{2} )$

where $\delta_{t}$ is the log intercept of the Gompertz model and $\gamma_{t}$ is the growth rate of the growth rate and$\  \  \gamma > 0$. Disturbance terms $\varepsilon_{t}$, $\eta_{t}$ and $\zeta_{t} \$represent randomness, level and slope, respectively and all are assumed to be normally and independently distributed (NID) with mean zero and variance $\sigma^{2}$. When $\sigma_{\zeta}^{2} > 0$ and $\sigma_{\eta}^{2} = 0$, the trend is an integrated random walk (IRW, SOURCE). The speed at which the trend adapts to change depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, defined as $q_{\zeta} = \frac{\sigma_{\zeta}^{2}}{\sigma_{\varepsilon}^{2}}$ for an IRW trend and $q_{\zeta} = 0$ for a deterministic trend, like equation (1).

## Forecasts

All these models can be handled using techniques based on state space models and the Kalman Filter (KF). For simplicity, we will exclude state-space notation from this document, but the TSGC package vignette describes this in detail ([link](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/tsgc/vignettes/tsgc_vignette.html)).

The KF outputs estimates and forecasts of the state vector $\left( \delta_{t} , \gamma_{t} \right)^{'}$. Estimates at time $t$ are conditional on information up to and including time $t$ are denoted $\left( \delta_{t | t} , \gamma_{t | t} \right)^{'}$, while predictions $j$ steps ahead are $\left( \delta_{t + j | t} , \gamma_{t + j | t} \right)^{'}$. The smoother, which estimates the state at time $t$ based on all $T$ observations in the series is denoted $\left( \delta_{t | T} , \gamma_{t | T} \right)^{'}$. We are interested in forecasting the saturation level at time $T$, conditional on information up to and including $T$, for predictions $\mathcal{l}$ steps ahead. Therefore, the forecasted trend in future values of $\ln {\  g}_{t}$ in the dynamic Gompertz model, equation (4), are given by:

(5) $\delta_{T \mathcal{+ l |} T} = \delta_{T | T} - \gamma_{T | T} \mathcal{l}$ , $\mathcal{l} = 1 , 2 , \ldots$

where $\mathcal{l}$ is the number of recursions (aka forecast horizon), $\delta_{T | T}$ and $\gamma_{T | T}$ are the KF estimates of $\delta_{T}$ and $\gamma_{T}$ at the end of the sample.

Forecasts of the trend in daily observations are then obtained from a recursion for the trend in their cumulative total, $Y_{t}$, defined by:

(6) $\overline{\mu}_{T \mathcal{+ l |} T} = {\  Y}_{T} \prod_{j = 1}^{\mathcal{l}} \left( 1 + g_{T \mathcal{+ l |} T} \right)$, $\mathcal{l} = 1 , 2 , \ldots$

where $g_{T \mathcal{+ l |} T} = e x p  \left( \delta_{T \mathcal{+ l |} T} \right)$ and $\mu_{T | T} = Y_{T}$.

# Univariate Forecasting with `tsgc`

In this section we provide a breakdown of the `tsgc` package in R, which implements a univariate model for time series growth curves-based A&E attendance forecasting. While we wait to access daily hospital datasets, we will use simulated daily estimates from publicly available datasets for model development purposes.

## Simulated Data

This analysis uses weekly data on A&E attendance from 32 hospitals providing acute healthcare services for NHS Scotland from 16 February 2015 to 26 January 2025 , with n=35,355 observations (link). For each hospital, we simulated daily estimates using weekday weights based on recent articles on A&E wait times (link), such that Mondays were slightly busier and Wednesday and Fridays were slightly less busy. Random noise (SD=10) was introduced to the weights such that all simulated estimates added up to their respective weekly totals. This resulted in a multi-level time series with n=109,186 observations with daily new and cumulative cases, which may be aggregated to regional or national levels. This dataset can be joined to publicly available spatial data, including hospital GPS locations and NHS Scotland health board boundaries (link), to easily pair with extreme weather variables for future multivariate models. 

## Forecasting A&E attendance in Scotland

For the purposes of this exercise, we will only focus on building a univariate model for A&E attendance from a single hospital within the Ayrshire and Arran health board – Crosshouse Hospital (site code A111H). The dataset includes variables for new cases and cumulative cases of A&E attendance. To avoid confounding, we will exclude data from the COVID-19 years and only examine data up until 1 February 2020.

```{r packages, echo=FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Install & load packages
library(tsgc)
library(here)
library(zoo)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(kableExtra)
library(ggplot2)
library(xts)

df <- read.csv('C:/Users/offne/OneDrive - University of Cambridge/III. Research/Data/2_Active_Data/201_heal/agy_adm4_NHS-Scotland_2015-2025_daily-hosptial-ae.csv')

# Select hospital
df <- df %>% 
  filter(sitecode=='A111H') %>% # relevant sites
  select(-c(sitecode, weekday))

# Set date type, create XTS object & select outcome
df$date <- as.Date(df$date, format = "%Y-%m-%d")  # Adjust format as needed
Y <- xts(df[ , -1], order.by = df$date)

```
```{r data, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
head(df)
```

Across time, Crosshouse Hospital averages 182 new A&E hospital attendees each day (min: 72; max: 265; SD=28). Please note that the `tsgc` model requires the data series to be in cumulative form and is loaded as an xts object with a date index. We will therefore use the **`c_NumberOfAttendanceEpisode`** variable to forecast new A&E cases. **Figure 1** illustrates the 7-day moving average of new A&E cases from February 2017 to February 2020 (discrete observations, not cumulative).The wave in June 2018 looks like a good place to test the TSGC model.

```{r fig_1, echo=FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 1: New Cases and their centered 7-day moving average for Crosshouse Hospital 16 Feb 2017 and 01 Feb 2020."}

# Subset desired dates and select outcome
Y <- Y["2017-02-16/2020-02-01"]
Y <- Y$c_NumberOfAttendancesEpisode

# Calculate the 7 day centered moving average
ma.cent <- zoo::rollmean(diff(Y), 7, align = "center") 

# Create df for plot (actual data vs. MA data)
d <- setNames(cbind(diff(Y), ma.cent), c('New Cases', 'Centered 7-day MA'))
df.f <- data.frame(Date = index(d), 
                   New.Cases = coredata(d[,1]),
                   Centered.7.day.MA = coredata(d[,2]))

# Plot Figure 1
ggplot(data = df.f, aes(x = Date)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = New.Cases, color = "Real data"), linewidth=0.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Centered.7.day.MA, color = "Centered 7 day MA"), linewidth=1) +
  scale_y_continuous(n.breaks = 10) +
  xlab("Day") +
  ylab("New cases") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "60 days") +
  scale_color_manual(name='', values=c('Real data'='black', 'Centered 7 day MA'='red')) +
  theme_light(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = c(.2, 0.85)) +
  theme(legend.title=element_text(size=2),legend.text=element_text(size=10)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 10),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

```

## Model parameters

We begin by specifying a number of options for the forecasting exercise, as defined below.

-   **`Y`** is the data, in the form of time series of cumulative confirmed cases. In this example the object holding this series is called `england`.

-   **`estimation.date.start`** is the date of the first observation in the sample to be used for estimating the model. By default, it is the first date in the `xts` object `Y`. We are interested in the period before the June 2018 wave, so our start date is 1 January 2018.

-   **`estimation.date.end`** is the date of the last observation in the sample to be used for estimating the model. By default, it is the last date in the `xts` object `Y`. We are interested in the period before the June 2018 wave, so our end date is 25 May 2018.

-   **`n.forecasts`** is the number of days or periods for which forecasts are to be made. E.g., if `n.forecasts = 14`, forecasts will be generated for up to 14 days following `estimation.date.end`.

-   **`q`** is the signal-to-noise ratio, which controls the smoothness of the estimated trend. A lower value will lead to more smoothness. By default, `q = 0.005` is used, which is known to ensure a good balance between the smoothness of the trend and the speed with which changes in estimates respond to new observations (Harvey & Kattuman, 2020). Alongside, `q` can be estimated and compared with the default value.

-   **`confidence.level`** sets the coverage of the confidence intervals for $\ln(g_t)$ which is then used to generate the prediction intervals for forecasts. Here, we use 0.68, corresponding to the probability that the forecast lies within one standard deviation of the point forecast.

-   **`plt.length`** sets a truncation date to enhance the clarity of plots, e.g. showing only the last 30 days of the estimation sample. The date range for plotting can be set as `plt.length` days upto `estimation.date.end`.

-   Optional: **`sea.type`** specifies the type of seasonality and can take `trigonometric` (default) or `none` if there is no seasonal component. 

-   Optional: **`sea.period`** can be used to set the seasonality period by days (default is `7` for weekly patterns), and is not required if `sea.type = 0`

```{r parameters, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}

# Set sample period (dates)
estimation.date.start <- as.Date("2018-01-01")
estimation.date.end <- as.Date("2018-05-25")

# Set forecast period (days)
n.forecasts <- 14

# Set smoothness, confidence levels & plot visibility
q <- 0.005
confidence.level <- 0.68
plt.length <- 30

# Seasonality parameters are excluded from this example

```

## Model fit

Now that we understand what the model will do, we begin by selecting the data series (`Y`) for the defined sample period. Then we estimate the model using a diffuse prior distribution for the initial state vector, using a signal-to-noise ratio of $0.005$ (maintained throughout this example). As mentioned, this value strikes a useful balance between the smoothness of the estimate of the slope parameter $\gamma$, and the speed with which it adapts to new observations.

```{r model_est, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# Subset sample period 
y <- Y[estimation.date.start <= index(Y) & index(Y) <= estimation.date.end]

# Fit model with subset & smoothing ratio
model <- SSModelDynamicGompertz$new(Y = y, q = q)
res <- model$estimate()

```

To enable forecast comparisons, create an evaluation sample. This is simply a subset from the actual data of cases **AFTER** the estimation period, converted to the log growth rate.

```{r eval_sample, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
# From the original data, subset dates greater than estimation end date and convert to growth rates
y.eval <- Y %>% 
  subset(index(.) > estimation.date.end) %>% # subset
  tsgc::df2ldl() # log growth rate conversion

```

## Results

We can now plot the forecast of the log of the growth rate ($\ln g_t$) of cumulative cases (`Y`). We can compare these forecasts to the actual $\ln g_t$ series by passing the output of our estimation (`res`) along with an evaluation sample (`y.eval`) to a plotting function. 

### Growth rates

We use `plot_forecast` to plot the $\ln(g_t)$ of the 14-day forecast (`res`), relative to the actual data (`y.eval`)

```{r fig_2, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap="Figure 2: Fourteen-day forecast of growth rate from 25 May 2018 for Crosshouse Hospital."}

# Compare growth rate of projected estimations (res) to actual cases (y.eval)
tsgc::plot_forecast(
  res = res, # projected data (model estimation sample & projection)
  y.eval = y.eval, # actual data (after estimation period)
  n.ahead = n.forecasts,
  plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
)
```

### New cases

We use `plot_new_cases` to plot the forecasts of new cases from 25 May 2018, with their prediction intervals.

```{r fig_3, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 3: Fourteen-day forecast of new cases from 25 May 2018 for Crosshouse Hospital"}

# Compare actual data from estimation period to estimated forecast, with confidence level
tsgc::plot_new_cases(
  res = res, # projected data (model estimation sample & projection)
  Y = y, # actual data (from estimation period)
  n.ahead = n.forecasts,
  confidence.level = confidence.level,
  date_format = "%Y-%m-%d",
  plt.start.date = estimation.date.end - plt.length
)
```

### Accuracy

To assess accuracy, we use the `plot_holdout` function to plot forecasts against the actual new cases, that have been held back from the estimation sample. The estimated forecasts are compared to the actual data within the forecast window (`Y.eval`) using mean absolute percentage error (MAPE).

Figure 4 shows that the forecasts were accurate over the 14-days, with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 7%. 

```{r fig_4, echo=TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.cap = "Figure 4: Accuracy of the fourteen-day forecast of new cases from 21 November 2021 for England."}

# Compare estimated forecast (res) to actual data within the forecast window (Y.eval)
tsgc::plot_holdout(res = res, 
                   Y = y,
                   Y.eval = Y[(estimation.date.end+0:n.forecasts)],
                   confidence.level = 0.68,
                   date_format = "%Y-%m-%d")
```
